title: ADR: fleet topology, roles, and the review-capacity ceiling
description:
Roles: coordinator (allocates, never edits code), builder (bead → PR), reviewer (lens-specific, never merges), operator (watches Operate signals, files incidents), retro (monthly, proposes beads). Persistent vs. per-run for each.

The number that actually governs the design: how many PRs can one human review well in a morning. Everything else — concurrency caps, nightly budget, how many repos are active at once — derives from that ceiling rather than from what the machine can do.

Record the anti-goal explicitly: the fleet exists to keep the queue moving, not to maximise output.
acceptance_criteria: ADR names every role, its permissions, and the derived caps. The caps are numbers, not adjectives.
close_reason: ADR 0006 written: five roles (coordinator/builder/reviewer/operator/retro), only the coordinator stateful. Ceiling derived from review capacity rather than compute — 8 reviewable PRs/day → caps of 6 builder PRs/night, 3 concurrent builders, 2 active repos/night. Caps are numbers so the retro can check them, and they move only on measured merged-without-edits data.

title: ADR: three-layer agent architecture — beads, blackbird, Claude Code
description:
The most valuable thing this ADR does is say what NOT to build. No home-grown message bus, no home-grown lock service, no home-grown agent registry — blackbird already ships all three with durability, expiry, fencing tokens, and an authenticated event journal.

Record the boundary: beads owns work state, blackbird owns coordination state, Claude Code owns execution. A fact lives in exactly one of them. Where they could overlap (bd claim vs. blackbird reservation) name which wins and why: bd claims the *work*, blackbird reserves the *files*.
acceptance_criteria: ADR in this repo and both templates. Every later bead in E7/E8 cites it. No component in the flywheel duplicates a blackbird capability.
close_reason: ADR 0004 written (docs/adr/0004-three-layer-agent-architecture.md): beads owns the work graph, blackbird owns coordination (identity, reservations, messages, journal), Claude Code owns execution. bd claims the work, blackbird reserves the files, both required before edit. Nothing blackbird already ships gets rebuilt.

title: Decide: do the non-goals still hold now that the flywheel has five repos?
description:
SPEC.md's non-goals rule out 'multi-repo orchestration dashboards, agent fleets, inter-agent protocols — that's the C1 version; the personal one must stay cheap enough to actually use.'

That was written when the flywheel had one instance. It now has two templates and three instances, and the epics filed alongside this bead propose exactly the things the non-goal names.

The argument for revising: the non-goal states a category ban but its stated reason is a cost test. 'Cheap enough to actually use' and 'if a gate gets bypassed twice, delete it or automate it' are the real constraints, and they are better constraints — they survive contact with a fourth project, which a category ban does not.

The argument for keeping it: category bans are enforceable and cost tests are not. 'Cheap enough' is exactly the sort of judgement that loses to enthusiasm at 11pm, and the non-goal exists to protect against a specific failure mode — building the platform instead of the products.

Proposed resolution: replace the category ban with an explicit budget. Every stage declares its standing cost in minutes per month and dollars per month; anything over budget for two consecutive retros gets deleted. Orchestration is then allowed exactly insofar as it pays for itself, and the writeup gains a better story than 'I decided not to.'
acceptance_criteria: SPEC.md non-goals rewritten or explicitly reaffirmed, with the reasoning recorded. If revised, every epic in this repo carries a standing-cost estimate and the retro checks them.
close_reason: Resolved: revise. ADR 0001 replaces the category ban with a cost test — every stage and epic declares a standing cost in minutes/dollars per month, over budget for two consecutive retros means deleted or automated. Fleets and inter-agent protocols scoped as fw-oef and fw-wb2. Binding constraint recorded as review capacity, not compute.

title: ADR: autonomy boundaries for unattended agents
description:
Written before the first unattended run, not after the first incident.

Allowed: create branches, commit, run gates, open PRs, comment on beads, file beads. Forbidden: merging, tagging, releasing, deploying, touching prod hosts, rotating secrets, force-push, editing the audit log. Bounded: a hard token/dollar budget per run and a wall-clock cap; exceeding either aborts and reports.

Also decide the failure posture: an unattended agent that cannot make the gate green closes nothing and leaves the bead open with a comment explaining where it stopped. No half-finished merges, no 'fixed the test by deleting it'.
acceptance_criteria: ADR in both templates. Every subsequent bead in this epic cites it. The forbidden list is enforced by permissions/hooks, not by hoping.
close_reason: ADR 0003 written (docs/adr/0003-autonomy-boundaries.md): unattended agents may branch/commit/gate/PR/comment/reserve; may not merge, tag, release, deploy, touch prod, read secrets, force-push, or rewrite the audit log. Hard token and wall-clock caps; failure leaves the bead open with a comment rather than closing it.

title: tools/watch: SLO prober that files incidents as GitHub issues + beads
description:
The second piece of real code in the project (tools/dora was the first). Stdlib-only Go, run on a schedule (GitHub Actions cron, or on the host itself).

Reads slo.yml, probes the target, and on a sustained breach opens a GitHub issue labelled `incident` plus a `bd` bead. Dedup by fingerprint (target + breach kind) so a two-hour outage is one incident, not 120. Records the /healthz version so Learn can attribute failures to a release.
acceptance_criteria: Breach → exactly one incident issue + one bead. Repeat breaches within the same window do not duplicate. Unit tests table-driven, no new deps.
close_reason: Shipped in flywheel-template c923070: tools/watch reads slo.yml, probes /healthz, files exactly one incident-labelled GitHub issue per (target, breach kind), deduped by a fingerprint marker embedded in the issue body rather than by title matching. Stateless — sustain windows are enforced by re-probing, not by remembering across invocations, so it runs identically from a workflow, a cron, or the host. Flat-YAML parsed in ~40 lines rather than taking the template's first dependency (ponytail comment names the ceiling and upgrade path). operate.yml runs it every 30min with a concurrency group so two probers never race. 16 subtests green, vet clean.

title: ADR: Operate is a first-class stage (five stages become six)
description:
Record why the personal flywheel needs an explicit Operate stage where the C1 write-up folded it into Release+Learn: at C1 tenants ran the artifact and their telemetry was someone else's job. Solo, nobody is watching unless something watches.

Cover: what Operate owns (SLOs, probes, incident lifecycle, rollback), what it does NOT own (dashboards-as-a-product, paging, on-call rotation), and the cost ceiling — if Operate costs more than a few minutes a month to keep running, it gets cut.
acceptance_criteria: docs/adr/ entry ~20 lines in both templates. SPEC.md stage table gains the row. WRITEUP.md structure updated to six.
close_reason: ADR 0002 written (docs/adr/0002-operate-is-a-stage.md): Operate becomes the sixth stage between Release and Learn, owning slo.yml, the prober, incident lifecycle, and post-deploy smoke/rollback. Paging, on-call, and dashboards-as-product explicitly out of scope.

title: Operate: promote the Release→Learn gap to a first-class stage
description:
Today the flywheel ends at 'binary on a host'. Nothing observes the running thing, so two of the four DORA metrics (change-failure rate, MTTR) are fed by hand-labelling GitHub issues `incident`. That is exactly the discipline-dependent process SPEC.md says to delete or automate.

Operate closes the loop: the deployed artifact reports on itself, breaches become incidents automatically, and Learn gets honest numbers instead of numbers that depend on remembering.
acceptance_criteria: Six stages documented in SPEC.md and WRITEUP.md. An SLO breach on a deployed instance files an incident with no human in the loop, and its recovery closes it. The router's dora.json shows a non-zero, un-hand-authored CFR and MTTR.

title: Fleet observability and the fleet-wide kill switch
description:
One view: every registered agent, what bead it holds, what territory it has reserved, how long it has held them, and what it has spent. Sources already exist — blackbird agents/reservations, bd in_progress, the agent audit log.

The kill switch from fw-lb8.6 goes fleet-wide here: one command stops every agent across every repo, releases reservations, and returns leased beads to ready. Checked at the top of every cycle. If stopping the fleet takes longer than a few seconds it is not a kill switch, it is a hope.
acceptance_criteria: Fleet view answers 'what is running right now' in one command. Kill switch verified by tripping it mid-cycle with three agents active: all stop, all reservations released, all beads back to ready, nothing corrupted.

title: Fleet budget: dollars and tokens allocated per repo, enforced
description:
A declared monthly budget, split across repos and roles, enforced at allocation time rather than discovered afterwards. A repo that burns its share pauses until the next window; the coordinator says so rather than failing quietly.

This is also the mechanism that makes ADR 0001's cost test real: every stage and every epic declares a standing cost, and the fleet is where those numbers get spent and measured. Feeds directly into fw-e7e.2.
acceptance_criteria: A deliberately starved repo pauses cleanly and reports why. Monthly spend per repo appears on the fleet dashboard next to what it produced.

title: Coordinator: allocate ready work across five repos under caps
description:
The fleet's only stateful actor. Each cycle: gather ready work across every flywheel repo, filter by budget and concurrency caps, route via the roster, spawn builders in isolated worktrees, respect merge-slot for merges, and escalate anything it cannot place.

It allocates and never edits code — that separation is what makes its decisions auditable and its failures survivable. Use 'bd swarm create' on epics rather than inventing an orchestration format.
acceptance_criteria: One coordinator run distributes work across at least three repos concurrently, produces green PRs, and leaves a complete decision log of what it allocated and what it declined, with reasons.

title: Agent fleet: many agents, five repos, one budget
description:
The layer above the protocol: not 'can two agents share a repo' but 'what is the whole fleet working on tonight, and what did it cost'.

This is the C1 capability the v1 spec deliberately refused, now in scope under a cost budget rather than a ban (ADR 0001). The honest version at personal scale is small: a coordinator, a handful of roles, concurrency caps low enough that a human can still review the output, and a single number for what it burned.

The real risk is not runaway agents. It is producing more plausible-looking PRs than one person can review properly — review capacity, not compute, is the binding constraint, and the fleet must be sized to it.
acceptance_criteria: One coordinator distributes ready work across all five repos overnight, inside a declared budget, with a live view of who is doing what and one command to stop everything. Sized so the morning's queue is reviewable in under an hour.

title: Work claims need leases: heartbeat, expiry, and reclaim
description:
'bd update --claim' is atomic but has no liveness. An agent that dies mid-bead leaves it claimed forever, and the fleet quietly starves.

Add a lease: claim carries a TTL, the working agent heartbeats, and an expired lease returns the bead to ready with a note recording who dropped it and where. Prefer implementing this in the flywheel's own run loop over patching bd, unless bd already has it — check first.
acceptance_criteria: Kill an agent mid-bead: within the TTL the bead is back in 'bd ready' with a note, no human involved, and the partial worktree is either cleaned up or explicitly flagged.
close_reason: Shipped 13cff31: tools/fleet lease layer. Confirmed first that bd has no lease support — --claim is atomic but has no liveness, and bd stale is day-granularity, far too coarse for a nightly fleet. Lease state lives in the bead's own metadata (beads owns claims, ADR 0004) so it survives the machine that took it. Claim refuses a live lease held by another agent; heartbeat refuses to extend someone else's, which stops a reclaimed agent waking up and editing alongside its replacement; reclaim returns expired leases to open with a note naming who dropped them and warning about stale worktrees, and deliberately leaves unleased in-progress beads alone because those are a human's work. VERIFIED LIVE against the real database: claim -> second agent refused -> heartbeat -> stale agent refused -> status countdown -> expire -> reclaim -> back to open with note. 9 tests.

title: Territory: blackbird file reservations before any edit
description:
The piece that makes parallel agents genuinely safe, and the reason worktrees alone are not enough: worktrees isolate edits but they do not isolate *merges*. Two agents can each be green in isolation and still produce an incoherent main.

Protocol: acquire the narrowest relevant reservation (exact file or subtree) before editing, hold a fencing token, renew while working, release on completion or abort. Overlap is refused at acquire time, so the conflict surfaces in seconds rather than at merge.

Expiry is the safety valve — a crashed agent's territory frees itself.
acceptance_criteria: Two agents told to edit the same file: the second is refused at reservation time, files a bead, and moves on. A killed agent's reservation expires and the territory becomes acquirable without manual cleanup.
notes:
Substrate verified live 2026-08-15 against the running blackbird daemon (MCP, 127.0.0.1:8081):
- agent_register returns actor_id + registration_token; the registration token authenticates subsequent calls as agent_token.
- reservation_acquire(exclusive, subtree:docs/adr, ttl 120s) → lease_id + fences [{conflict_key: subtree:docs/adr, counter: 1}] + expires_at.
- A SECOND registered agent requesting exact:docs/adr/0001-....md was refused with LEASE_CONFLICT — overlap detection works ACROSS granularities (exact-inside-subtree), which is the property this bead depends on.
- reservation_release with lease_id + fences returned released_at.
Conclusion: territory needs no new code, only convention + wiring. Remaining work here is the acquire-before-edit discipline in the agent loop and the expiry/crash path.

title: Agent identity: registration, naming convention, token custody
description:
Every flywheel agent registers with blackbird before it does anything: project_key = absolute repo path, stable agent_name, registration token retained so the same identity survives restarts.

Naming convention matters more than it looks — it is what makes the audit log and the fleet view readable. Proposed: <repo>/<role>[-<lens>], e.g. router/builder, router/reviewer-security, fleet/coordinator.

Token custody: registration tokens live in the run sandbox or XDG state, never in the repo, never in a worktree that might get committed.
acceptance_criteria: An agent killed and restarted resumes the same blackbird identity. No token has ever been committed — verified by gitleaks (see fw-l8k.4).
notes: Verified: blackbird_agent_register is idempotent per (project_key, agent_name) and returns a registration_token for resuming the same identity. Naming convention proven readable in practice: registered flywheel/builder and flywheel/reviewer-security against project_key=/home/drspeedracer/Workspace/agentic-flywheel. Token custody is the open part — they must live in XDG state or the run sandbox, never the repo.

title: Inter-agent protocol: identity, territory, claims, and handoffs
description:
Before there can be a fleet there has to be a contract. Two agents editing the same repo without one is not a fleet, it is a race.

The substrate already exists and does not need building. Three layers, no overlap:

  beads       — the work graph: what exists, what blocks what, who claimed it
  blackbird   — the coordination bus: agent identity, file reservations with fencing
                tokens, conversations, acks, and a tamper-evident event journal
                (daemon already running locally, MCP-connected, ships a bd probe)
  Claude Code — the execution substrate: worktrees, subagents, skills, scheduled runs

The protocol is the set of rules that binds them. Almost all of this epic is wiring and convention, not new services — which is the only reason it fits inside the flywheel's cost budget.
acceptance_criteria: Two agents work the same repo concurrently without corrupting each other: territory reserved before edit, claims leased and reclaimable, handoffs acknowledged, every action in the journal. Proven by a conformance harness, not by it having gone fine once.

title: tools/dora → tools/learn: add agent-effectiveness metrics
description:
Extend the collector (still stdlib, still no deps) with metrics that describe how the work got done:

- first-pass gate rate: PRs green on the first CI run
- rework: commits pushed after the first review, and review round-trips per PR
- intent-to-merge lead time: bead created → PR merged (DORA's lead time starts at first commit and misses the whole Intent stage)
- review escape rate: defects found later that pre-push review saw or missed (needs the E3 ledger)
- autonomous share: PRs opened unattended, and what fraction merged without human edits
acceptance_criteria: dora.json grows an 'agent' section, backfilled across the router's existing PR history so there is a trend line on day one rather than in a month.

title: Learn v2: measure the agent, not just the code
description:
DORA measures the software. Nothing measures the thing that is actually novel here — that an agent wrote most of it.

Nobody has good public numbers on agentic development: what fraction of PRs land green first time, how much rework a change takes, what a merged PR costs in tokens, whether AI review catches things or just talks. This project is already generating that data and throwing it away.

Public DORA for personal projects was the memorable move. Public agent-effectiveness metrics is the version of that move nobody else has made.
acceptance_criteria: One dashboard with DORA plus agent metrics across every flywheel repo, populated automatically, with at least one month of real history before anything is claimed publicly.

title: Review findings ledger: record every finding and what became of it
description:
Append-only .flywheel/review.jsonl. Each finding: id, lens, file, severity, the claim, and the disposition — accepted-and-fixed, rejected-with-reason, or ignored.

Then the interesting part: correlate. A defect later found by CI, by Operate, or by a human is tagged with whether review saw it first. That yields escape rate, which is the only honest measure of whether AI review is earning its place in the loop.
acceptance_criteria: Ledger populated automatically by the pre-push panel. tools/learn reports findings-per-PR, acceptance rate, and escape rate. One month of data before any claim about review value goes in the writeup.

title: Review panel: correctness, security, and simplicity lenses instead of one reviewer
description:
Replace the single ponytail-review pre-push call with three subagents given genuinely different briefs, findings merged and deduped before display.

Correctness: does this do what the bead said, and what breaks it. Security: input handling, secrets, dependency surface, authz assumptions. Simplicity (ponytail): is there a shorter thing that works, is anything speculative.

Keep it advisory and keep it under the time budget that makes a pre-push hook survivable. If three lenses make the hook slow enough to skip, run them in parallel or cut to two — a bypassed gate is worse than no gate.
acceptance_criteria: Three lenses run in parallel at pre-push, output is one deduped list, and the hook still finishes fast enough that it never gets skipped. Measured against the router's history: does the panel catch things the single reviewer missed?

title: Validate v2: a review panel, a findings ledger, and a supply chain
description:
The gate is real but thin: lint, unit tests, and one advisory AI reviewer. Three things are missing that a team would have given you for free — diversity of review perspective, any memory of what review found, and any statement about what is actually inside the artifact you publish.

The findings ledger is the sleeper item here: it is what turns 'the AI reviewer is useful' from an anecdote in the writeup into a measured claim.
acceptance_criteria: Pre-push review runs multiple lenses and every finding is recorded with its eventual fate. Releases ship an SBOM and a signature. The router's published claims about review value are backed by the ledger, not by memory.

title: Audit log + kill switch for every autonomous action
description:
Append-only .flywheel/agent-log.jsonl: run id, bead, model, start/end, tools invoked, files touched, tokens, outcome. The agent may write to it and may not rewrite it.

Kill switch: one command (or one committed file) that stops all scheduled agentic runs immediately, checked at the top of every run. If you cannot stop the fleet in five seconds you do not have a fleet, you have a problem.
acceptance_criteria: Kill switch verified by tripping it mid-run. Audit log is complete enough to reconstruct any night's work, and feeds the cost metrics in Learn v2.
notes:
PROGRESS (not done): tools/flywheel/guard.sh shipped — kill switch + audit log.
Verified standalone: check exits 0 runnable / 1 stopped; repo and fleet stop files with fleet taking precedence; resume clears; log emits valid JSONL with quote/tab escaping (8/8 checks pass).
Committed .gitattributes with merge=union on the log so parallel agents append without conflicting; STOP is gitignored so stopping the fleet never requires a push.
REMAINING for acceptance: (1) trip the kill switch MID-RUN against a live agent, not standalone; (2) wire the log into cost metrics (fw-e7e.2).

title: Nightly scheduled run of /flywheel-next with a hard budget cap
description:
The skill on a cron. One repo to start (the router), one bead per night, capped spend.

Open question worth deciding in this bead: cloud-scheduled agent vs. a cron on the linux box the router already needs for Operate. The box is cheaper and can see the deployed instance; the cloud runner is more reliable and leaves better logs.
acceptance_criteria: Seven consecutive unattended nights with no manual babysitting. Budget cap demonstrably enforced — one run should be deliberately starved to prove the abort path works.

title: /flywheel-next skill: claim a ready bead, build it in a worktree, open the PR
description:
The single unit of autonomous work, usable interactively first and only then on a schedule.

Steps: bd ready → pick highest-priority unblocked bead → bd update --claim → git worktree add → read SPEC.md + the bead + relevant ADRs → implement under ponytail discipline → run the full local gate → open a PR referencing the bead → comment the outcome on the bead → remove the worktree.

Ships in both templates so any flywheel repo gets it on clone.
acceptance_criteria: Run by hand against a real bead in the router or brax repo, it produces a green, reviewable PR with no manual intervention. Idempotent: a second run picks a different bead and never double-claims.
notes:
PROGRESS (not done): .claude/skills/flywheel-next/SKILL.md written — the full unit of autonomous work: guard check, blackbird identity, bd claim, territory reservation (fail closed on LEASE_CONFLICT), worktree, gate, PR, release, report, plus an explicit cannot-finish path that leaves the bead open and escalates.
Encodes ADR 0003 boundaries (never merge/tag/deploy/secrets/force-push) and ADR 0004 layering.
REMAINING for acceptance: run it by hand against a real bead in the router or brax repo and confirm it produces a green reviewable PR unattended; confirm a second run picks a different bead and never double-claims.

title: Autonomous loop: agents that advance the board while you are not at the keyboard
description:
Today the flywheel is one agent, one session, one human sitting in front of it. Every primitive needed to change that is already installed and unused: worktree isolation, subagents, scheduled runs, and bd's own multi-agent machinery (swarm, gate, merge-slot).

The unit of autonomy is deliberately small: take one ready bead, do it in an isolated worktree, put a PR up, stop. The human still merges. The value is not 'the agent builds the product' — it is that the queue drains overnight and you wake up to reviewable diffs instead of an empty branch list.

NOTE: this epic knowingly reopens a SPEC.md non-goal ('agent fleets'). See fw-2bv for the argument that the non-goal should become a cost test rather than a category ban.
acceptance_criteria: A scheduled unattended run picks a ready bead, produces a green PR, and comments on the bead — with a budget cap, an audit log, and a one-command kill switch. Measured over a month: PRs opened unattended, and what fraction were mergeable as-is.

title: Router adopts Operate end-to-end on the linux box
description:
The outstanding dependency from SPEC.md M3 ('host deploy waits on the box being set up') plus everything above, proven on the pilot.

Deploy the router to the linux box under systemd, point tools/watch at it, and let it run long enough to record at least one real incident and recovery — inducing one deliberately is fair.
acceptance_criteria: Router running under systemd on the box; one genuine incident recorded, auto-closed, and visible in the router's dora.json without any hand-editing.

title: Post-deploy smoke + auto-rollback in deploy.sh
description:
deploy.sh currently pulls a binary and restarts a systemd unit — it never checks whether the thing it just deployed works.

Add: after restart, poll /healthz until healthy or timeout; on timeout, restore the previous binary, restart, and file an incident. Keep the previous release on disk for exactly this.
acceptance_criteria: A deliberately broken build deployed to the box rolls itself back and leaves an incident bead behind. Verified once for real, not just in a test.
close_reason: Shipped in flywheel-template: deploy.sh keeps the outgoing binary as <bin>.prev, polls /healthz after restart for SMOKE_TIMEOUT, and on failure restores the previous build, restarts, and exits 1. Rollback is a local copy rather than a re-download because the network is what you cannot count on mid-rollback. Unset HEALTHZ warns loudly instead of passing silently. VERIFIED locally end-to-end against a deliberately broken build (v1-good -> bad v2 -> smoke fail -> v1-good restored, exit 1) plus happy path and warning path; added ASSET_URL to make that possible without a host. NOT yet verified on the real linux box — that is fw-wma.6, which is blocked on the box existing.

title: Auto-close incidents on recovery so MTTR is measured, not estimated
description:
The other half of tools/watch. When the probe recovers and holds for a settle window, close the incident issue and the bead with a close reason naming the recovery time.

This is the change that makes MTTR a real number: today it measures how fast you remember to close a GitHub issue.
acceptance_criteria: A simulated outage-then-recovery produces an incident with open and close timestamps that tools/dora reads into a real MTTR figure.
close_reason: Shipped with fw-wma.3 in the same tool: on a healthy probe, watch looks for an open incident matching any breach-kind fingerprint, waits recover_after, re-probes, and closes with a comment stamping the recovery time. A recovery that does not hold leaves the incident open and reports 'flapping'. This is what makes MTTR a measured open→close span rather than a measure of how fast someone clicked Close. Covered by TestRun/recovery_that_holds_closes_the_incident and .../does_not_hold_leaves_it_open.

title: SLO contract: docs/slo.yml + /healthz convention in both templates
description:
A tiny declarative file the prober reads, and one endpoint every flywheel service exposes.

slo.yml: target availability, p99 latency budget, probe URL, probe interval, error budget window. /healthz: 200 + JSON {status, version, uptime_s} — version matters because it lets Learn attribute an incident to a release.
acceptance_criteria: slo.yml present and documented in both templates; template main.go/main.py serve /healthz; the router already satisfies the contract or gets a bead to.
close_reason: Shipped in flywheel-template c923070: docs/slo.yml declares the contract (url, breach_after, recover_after, latency_budget, availability_target) and healthz.go provides a drop-in Healthz handler serving {status,version,uptime_s} — kept when a project replaces main.go. Version is ldflag-injected so Learn can attribute an incident to a release. Deliberate call: /healthz returns 200 even when degraded, because a 5xx is indistinguishable from the process being down; the body carries the detail. 3 subtests.

title: Fleet dashboard section: what the fleet did last night, and what it cost
description:
Extends the fw-e7e.4 fleet roll-up with the agent side: PRs opened per repo, merged without human edits, escalations raised, budget consumed against allocation, drills passed.

This is the artifact that makes the whole v2 story legible to someone who has thirty seconds — and the one nobody else has published.
acceptance_criteria: Public page, built from committed data, no backend. A stranger can tell within thirty seconds what a fleet of agents did to five repositories last week and what it cost.

title: Chaos drill: kill agents mid-flight and prove the fleet recovers
description:
The router earned its credibility from a chaos harness that proved the resilience claims run rather than compile. The fleet deserves the same treatment, and the parallel is worth naming in the writeup: the flywheel applies its own pilot project's engineering standard to itself.

Drills: kill a builder mid-edit, kill the coordinator mid-allocation, expire a reservation under load, saturate the merge slot, exhaust a repo's budget mid-run. Each has a defined correct outcome.
acceptance_criteria: Every drill runs from one command and asserts recovery. A drill failure files a bead automatically. Recorded once as a terminal demo for the writeup.

title: Fleet roster: capability registry and work routing
description:
Which agents exist, what they are for, and how a bead finds the right one.

bd beads already carry a --skills field and labels (stage:*, lang:*, instance:*); agents registered in blackbird already carry names and project scope. Routing is the join: a bead labelled lang:python goes to an agent that knows the uv/ruff/pytest template, a bead labelled stage:validate goes to a reviewer.

Keep the roster a committed file, not a database. It should be readable in ten seconds and diffable in review.
acceptance_criteria: A newly filed bead is routed to a correct agent with no human assignment, across at least three repos and two languages.

title: Protocol conformance harness: prove the rules hold under failure
description:
Every claim in this epic is a claim about behaviour under failure, and failure is exactly what does not get tested by things going fine.

Harness runs two real agents against a scratch repo and asserts: overlapping reservation refused; killed agent's lease reclaimed; killed agent's reservation expired; unacknowledged handoff escalates; every action present in the journal. Run it in CI on the templates.
acceptance_criteria: The harness fails loudly if any protocol rule regresses, and runs on every PR to the templates.

title: Cross-repo dependencies via bd bead gates
description:
bd gates already support cross-rig bead awaits (await_id '<rig>:<bead-id>'), which is exactly the primitive needed for 'brax cannot adopt Operate until the template ships it'.

Wire the real dependencies that exist today between the five repos, and decide gates-vs-federation: gates are cheap and one-directional, federation syncs whole databases. Start with gates; reach for federation only if the fleet coordinator genuinely needs one queryable graph.
acceptance_criteria: A template bead closing unblocks beads in all three instances automatically. The decision between gates and federation is recorded with the reason.

title: Message contract: handoff, finding, escalate — and what must be acknowledged
description:
One blackbird conversation per bead, per blackbird's own guidance. A small closed set of message types, because an open-ended chat between agents is a token bonfire with no audit value:

  handoff   builder → reviewer: branch, bead, what changed, what to look at. ACK REQUIRED.
  finding   reviewer → builder: one finding, severity, file:line, claim. Ack optional.
  escalate  any agent → human: blocked, over budget, or genuinely uncertain. ACK REQUIRED.
  status    heartbeat-ish progress note. No ack.

Escalate is the important one. An agent that cannot tell you it is stuck will instead do something confident and wrong.
acceptance_criteria: A build→review→fix cycle runs entirely through the contract with no free-text improvisation. An unacknowledged handoff older than the TTL escalates to the human rather than stalling silently.

title: Publish the router blog post (outstanding from M4)
description:
Drafted since 2026-08-08, pending a voice pass. The oldest open thread in the project.

It is worth shipping before the v2 work lands, since it is the artifact that describes the pilot as it actually was.
acceptance_criteria: Published and linked from the router README and the fleet dashboard.

title: WRITEUP v2: six stages, autonomy boundaries, and what changed at three projects
description:
The current draft is good and is about to be out of date. The revision has a better story than the original because it has a second act: what the flywheel looked like at one project versus what it needed at three.

New material: the sixth stage and why solo work needs it named; the autonomy boundaries ADR and the argument that constraining agents is what makes them usable unattended; measured agent-effectiveness numbers rather than the anecdote about eleven PRs; the non-goals revision and what it cost to be wrong the first time.

Keep the voice pass that the current draft is still waiting on.
acceptance_criteria: Published, six stages, every quantitative claim traceable to committed data.

title: Sync both templates to v2, at parity
description:
The Go and Python templates are already slightly divergent (the Python one has no tools/ and reuses the Go collector via 'go run'). Everything in E1-E5 needs to land in both, or the Python one quietly becomes the second-class citizen and brax-tennis-rl stops benefiting.

Decide the sharing strategy as part of this: shared tools invoked cross-language (as learn.yml already does) versus duplicated implementations. The first is cheaper and already proven.
acceptance_criteria: Both templates carry every stage. A fresh clone of either bootstraps in under the 30-minute budget — re-measure it, since the last figure (2m55s) predates all of this.

title: flywheel doctor: tell a repo which stages it is missing, then install them
description:
The answer to template drift, and the piece that makes the template a living system rather than a snapshot.

Run in any repo: check for each stage's artifacts (SPEC.md, ADR dir, lefthook, pr.yml, release.yml, learn.yml, slo.yml, beads, skills), report what is absent or out of date against the current template, and offer to add it. Idempotent, and it never clobbers local edits without saying so.

This is also how the router and brax-tennis-rl adopt everything in E1-E5 without hand-copying files three times.
acceptance_criteria: Run against all three instance repos it correctly identifies the gaps. Adoption of one full stage in one command, verified on brax-tennis-rl.

title: Distribution: keep five repos on one flywheel, and tell the story
description:
A template repo solves onboarding once and then rots: the three instances forked from it at three different versions and none of them will ever get the improvements filed in these epics unless something carries them forward.

This epic is the boring infrastructure that makes everything else actually reach the projects, plus the artifacts that make the work legible to the people it is aimed at.
acceptance_criteria: Any flywheel repo can report what it is missing and adopt it in one command. The writeup describes six stages and is published.

title: /flywheel-retro: the monthly ritual, automated but human-approved
description:
SPEC.md is candid that the monthly retro is 'a calendar reminder, not automation' — which by the project's own rule makes it a process that will quietly stop happening.

Monthly scheduled agent: read the dora.json git history, the closed beads and their close reasons, the review ledger, the bypass counts, and the incidents. Produce a short retro document and a proposed set of beads. Proposed, not created — the human approves the list, and that approval is the whole ritual.

Insight → Intent, without depending on remembering.
acceptance_criteria: Three consecutive months of retros produced without a human initiating them, each yielding at least one bead that got worked. If the proposals are consistently ignored, delete the skill rather than keep pretending.

title: Fleet dashboard: every flywheel repo on one page
description:
There are five repos in the flywheel now (two templates, three instances) and the dashboard shows them one at a time.

One page: per-repo DORA, agent metrics, open bead counts, current Operate status, last release. Terminal-styled, same as now. This is also the honest answer to the multi-repo non-goal — a static roll-up page is not an orchestration platform.
acceptance_criteria: jamesponwith.github.io shows the whole fleet at a glance, built from each repo's committed dora.json, no backend.

title: Gate-bypass detector: enforce the bypassed-twice rule with data
description:
SPEC.md's best line is 'if a gate gets bypassed twice, delete it or automate it'. Right now nothing counts bypasses, so the rule is a slogan.

Count: --no-verify commits, skipped hooks, force merges, admin-merged PRs, quarantined-test deadlines missed. Surface it in the retro. A gate over its bypass budget gets an automatic bead proposing its own deletion.
acceptance_criteria: Bypass counts on the dashboard. At least one gate gets deleted or automated because the data said so — and that story goes in the writeup.

title: Cost accounting: tokens and dollars per merged PR
description:
The number every engineering org will need within a year and almost nobody is measuring on their own work.

Source it from the autonomous run audit log (E2) plus whatever the interactive sessions expose. Report cost per merged PR, per bead, and per feature, tracked over time — the interesting question is not the absolute figure but whether it falls as the conventions get better.
acceptance_criteria: Cost per merged PR on the dashboard with a trend. A defensible sentence in the writeup about what an agent-built feature actually costs.

title: Signal intake: CVEs, dependency alerts, failed schedules, and incidents become beads
description:
A small workflow that turns external events into Intent: dependabot/security advisories, failed scheduled workflow runs, and incidents raised by Operate all file beads with enough context to act on.

Deduplicate hard. The failure mode is an inbox nobody reads, which is worse than no inbox.
acceptance_criteria: Each signal type demonstrably files exactly one actionable bead. A week with no signals files nothing.

title: Bead lint in CI: no bead, no build — enforced
description:
Check on every PR: the branch or a commit references an existing bead id, and that bead is open and claimed. Check on merge: the bead gets closed with a close reason (the router's existing beads all have good ones — codify the habit before it decays).

Advisory for a fortnight, then blocking. If it turns out to be annoying enough to bypass twice, delete it — that is the rule.
acceptance_criteria: PRs without a valid bead reference are flagged. Merged beads without close reasons are reported weekly.

title: /flywheel-plan: SPEC section → epic + child beads + dependency graph
description:
bd already accepts a JSON plan via 'bd create --graph' — this skill is the thing that writes one.

Read a named SPEC.md section, propose an epic with children, acceptance criteria per child, and the dependency edges between them. Always dry-run first and show the graph for approval; the human edits the plan, not the beads afterwards.

This bead is its own dogfood: the epic you are reading was hand-built, and the skill should be able to reproduce something close to it from SPEC.md.
acceptance_criteria: Run against a fresh SPEC section it produces a plan a human approves with light edits. Reproducing this repo's own epics from SPEC.md is the acceptance demo.

title: Intent v2: specs that decompose themselves, and signals that arrive as beads
description:
Intent is the stage with the least machinery and the most hand-work. Every bead in every repo so far was typed by a human. Every ADR was written because someone remembered. The one rule that exists ('no bead, no build') is enforced by conscience.

Two moves: make decomposition cheap (spec section in, dependency graph of beads out) and make Intent receive input from outside your own head (CVEs, failing schedules, dependency alerts, incidents from Operate).
acceptance_criteria: A SPEC.md section becomes a reviewed epic-plus-children graph in one command. External signals arrive as beads without a human transcribing them. The no-bead-no-build rule is checked by CI rather than by memory.

title: Deeper test rungs: race detection, fuzz corpus, property tests
description:
The component suite proved its worth by catching a race CI found and the local suite did not (per the writeup). Institutionalise that.

Go: -race in the CI unit job, a checked-in fuzz seed corpus for parsers/routers, short fuzz runs per PR and longer ones on the weekly schedule. Python: hypothesis for the equivalent surface.
acceptance_criteria: -race on by default in CI for both the templates and the router. At least one fuzz target with a seed corpus. A weekly longer run that files a bead on any new crasher.

title: Security gate in pr.yml: secret scanning + dependency vulnerabilities
description:
gitleaks on the diff, govulncheck for Go, pip-audit (or uv's equivalent) for Python. Blocking on secrets, advisory on vulnerabilities until the noise level is known.

Complements the pre-push security lens: the lens reasons about the code, this checks the facts.
acceptance_criteria: Both templates gate on it. A planted test secret is caught. Vulnerability findings file beads rather than silently failing the build.

title: Supply chain: SBOM, keyless signing, and provenance on every release
description:
goreleaser already does most of this — enabling it is configuration, not code. Add SBOM generation, cosign keyless signing via the Actions OIDC token, and SLSA provenance attestation to release.yml.

Cheap to turn on, hard to argue with, and it makes the release stage look like it was built by someone who has shipped software into a regulated environment. Which is the point.
acceptance_criteria: Next router release carries an SBOM, a signature verifiable with cosign, and a provenance attestation. The verification command is in the README and has been run once by a human.

title: Overnight digest: one message with what was attempted, what went green, what it cost
description:
Unattended work you have to go looking for is unattended work you will stop trusting.

One digest per run: beads attempted, PRs opened with links, gate results, tokens and dollars spent, anything abandoned and why. Delivered somewhere unavoidable — the same place the DORA dashboard lives is a reasonable default.
acceptance_criteria: A single artifact per night that answers 'was that worth it?' in under thirty seconds of reading.

title: Parallel agents: N ready beads → N worktrees, merges serialized by bd merge-slot
description:
The scaling step, gated on the single-agent loop being boring first.

bd already ships the primitives: swarm for structured epics, gate for async coordination, merge-slot for serialized conflict resolution. Fan out one agent per independent ready bead, isolate each in its own worktree, and let merge-slot make the merge queue single-file so two agents never rebase into each other.

Cap concurrency low (2-3). The failure mode to watch for is not conflicts, it is three plausible-looking PRs that nobody has the attention to review properly.
acceptance_criteria: Three independent beads worked in parallel produce three green PRs with zero cross-contamination. A deliberately conflicting pair is serialized by merge-slot and the loser files a bead rather than force-merging.

title: Drift watch: instances notice when they fall behind the template
description:
Weekly workflow in each instance: diff the flywheel-owned files against the current template and file a bead listing what changed upstream. Not automatic adoption — a bead, so the human decides.

Complements flywheel doctor: doctor is pull, drift watch is notify.
acceptance_criteria: A change to the template produces beads in all three instances within a week, with no false positives on locally-customised files.

title: ADR drift check: decisions that got re-derived without being recorded
description:
Advisory only. Flag PRs that add a dependency, change a public interface, or touch an area an existing ADR covers, without an accompanying ADR or a reference to one.

The failure this prevents is the one the whole Intent stage exists for: re-deriving a decision six weeks later because nobody wrote down why.
acceptance_criteria: Runs on every PR, never blocks, and its flags are correct often enough to be worth reading. If it is wrong more than half the time it gets deleted.

title: Interface-first: a design step for anything larger than one session
description:
The one genuinely missing part of the classic cycle. ADRs capture decisions, SPEC.md captures scope, but nothing captures shape — the types, the API surface, the boundaries — before implementation starts. With an agent doing the typing, shape is exactly where a human's judgement is worth the most and costs the least.

Convention, not tooling: a multi-session bead gets a short design note (signatures and boundaries, no prose) approved before code. Add it to CLAUDE.md; add a design-notes section to the bead template.
acceptance_criteria: Documented in both templates' CLAUDE.md. Used on the next feature bigger than one session and judged honestly in the retro: did it help, or was it ceremony?

title: Flaky test detection and quarantine
description:
The router already ate one decision-log test flake. A flake fixed by hand once is a flake that will come back.

Detect: reruns on failure, and a test that passes on rerun gets tagged. Quarantine: move to a non-blocking job and file a bead automatically, with a deadline — a quarantined test that is still quarantined in two weeks gets deleted, per the bypassed-twice rule.
acceptance_criteria: A deliberately flaky test is auto-detected, quarantined, and beaded without a human noticing it first.
